design_detail: Phase 3, randomized (1:1, stratified by site), double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group confirmatory trial (MAPP2; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04077437) at 13 sites (11 in the United States, 2 in Israel; institutional and private), recruiting from 21 August 2020 to 18 May 2022 (last visit 2 November 2022). 104 adults with moderate or severe PTSD (CAPS-5 total severity of 28 or more), off psychiatric medicines, received the same manualized therapy as in MAPP1 with MDMA or an inactive placebo in three 8-hour dosing sessions about a month apart, after three 90-minute preparation sessions and each followed by three 90-minute integration sessions. Primary end point: change in CAPS-5 total severity from baseline to 18 weeks (6 to 8 weeks after the third session), by blinded independent assessors over video; key secondary: SDS; blinding survey at study termination. Funded by MAPS with support from the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation and organized by MAPS PBC. An Author Correction (Nat Med 30, 3382; 7 October 2024) added 14 members of the MAPP2 Study Collaborator Group, previously listed only in the Supplementary Information, to the article's main list of collaborators; the notice describes no other change.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with moderate or severe PTSD off psychiatric medicines, adding MDMA to three sessions of the same manualized therapy lowered clinician-rated PTSD symptoms and functional impairment at 18 weeks more than adding an inactive placebo; how often participants identified their allocation by the end of the study; and which adverse events were more frequent with MDMA during treatment.
cannot_establish: How much of the difference is due to MDMA's pharmacology rather than participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations (94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified their group; expectancy was not measured); whether benefits last beyond about 2 months after the last session; how the treatment compares with trauma-focused psychotherapies or SSRIs; rare or delayed harms (53 people given MDMA over about 3 months); or effects in the people excluded (high suicide risk, personality disorders, cardiovascular disease, substance use disorders other than alcohol or cannabis in the previous year, and severe or moderate alcohol or cannabis use disorder).

sample.recruitment: 324 people consented after a phone screen and were screened; 203 were excluded, 121 enrolled, 17 excluded after enrollment (12 not meeting the criteria, 1 declined, 4 for other reasons) and 104 randomized, 53 to MDMA and 51 to placebo (Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1). Recruitment methods are not described in the main text; the registry's participant flow gives print and internet advertisements, referrals from other treatment providers and word of mouth (registry record, Participant Flow).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults aged 18 or older with DSM-5 current PTSD on the CAPS-5, a CAPS-5 total severity of 28 or more and symptoms for at least 6 months, tapered off all psychiatric medicines before baseline; full criteria only in the Supplementary Methods (PDF, not read) (Methods › Participants). The Discussion names the exclusion of people with a current, serious, imminent suicide risk, comorbid personality disorders and underlying cardiovascular disease, of any substance use disorder other than cannabis or alcohol in the 12 months before enrollment, and of severe or moderate (in early remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorder (Discussion, 4th and 6th paragraphs). The registry's current text adds willingness to stay overnight after each session and the same ecstasy-use exclusion as MAPP1's (more than 10 uses in 10 years, or any use in the 6 months before the first session), but that exclusion entered the record only on 28 October 2024 (version 38): the versions current during the trial excluded only current illegal drug use (registry record, Eligibility; History of Changes).
sample.demographics: MDMA vs placebo (Table 1): mean age 38.2 (SD 11.0) vs 40.0 (9.6); female at birth 32 (60.4%) vs 42 (82.4%); Hispanic or Latino 17 (32.1%) vs 11 (21.6%); White 37 (69.8%) vs 32 (62.7%); overall 35 of 104 (33.7%) other than White and 28 of 104 (26.9%) Hispanic or Latino; mean PTSD duration 16.3 vs 16.1 years; dissociative subtype 13 (24.5%) vs 11 (21.6%); comorbid major depression 49 (92.5%) vs 51 (100%); veterans 9 (17.0%) vs 7 (13.7%); baseline CAPS-5 39.4 (6.6) vs 38.7 (6.7); moderate PTSD 13 (24.5%) vs 15 (29.4%); BDI-II 25.4 vs 25.5; lifetime MDMA use 22 (41.5%) vs 26 (51.0%), in the past 10 years 13 (24.5%) vs 18 (35.3%); earlier sertraline 15 (28.3%) vs 10 (19.6%); earlier CBT 15 (28.3%) vs 14 (27.5%), prolonged exposure 2 (3.8%) vs 0, cognitive processing therapy 1 vs 1.
sample.attrition: MDMA: 1 of 53 (1.9%) stopped treatment, after the third session. Placebo: 8 of 51 (15.7%) stopped, 5 after the first session (3 chose to stop, 1 chose to stop before any outcome data and was excluded from the modified ITT set, 1 because of an adverse event) and 3 after the second (2 chose to stop, 1 because of an adverse event) (Fig. 1; Discussion, 3rd paragraph). The de jure analysis left out 12 outcome measurements taken after treatment had stopped (1 MDMA, 11 placebo) and one placebo 18-week CAPS-5 with missing item-level data, leaving 52 vs 42 at the primary end point (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1). The registry gives completed 52 vs 42 and not completed 1 vs 9.
sample.selection_effects: As in MAPP1, volunteers willing to stop psychiatric medicines and stay overnight in a trial of MDMA, with expectations not measured; almost half had used MDMA before (48 of 104), which may help them recognize its effects. The sample was more ethnically and racially diverse than MAPP1 but excluded high suicide risk, personality disorders, cardiovascular disease and most substance use disorders.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug, MDMA or an inactive placebo, in three 8-hour dosing sessions about a month apart, each as an initial dose followed 1.5 to 2 hours later by a supplemental half-dose, with identical therapy by trained two-person teams (at least one licensed therapist) following the MAPS treatment manual; procedures stated to be consistent with MAPP1 (the drug's manufacture is not described in the main text). Within the MDMA arm three participants did not have the planned increase in sessions 2 and 3 and two had dose-timing errors (Supplementary Table 2, not read) (Methods › Procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth, a split dose per session; session 1: 80 mg followed by a supplemental 40 mg; sessions 2 and 3: 120 mg followed by 60 mg; the supplemental half-dose 1.5 to 2 hours after the initial dose; the control arm received an inactive placebo on the same schedule (Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorders other than alcohol or cannabis in the previous 12 months were excluded, as were severe or moderate (in early remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorders (Discussion, 4th paragraph); baseline AUDIT and DUDIT scores are not given in Table 1; moderate risk of alcohol or substance use disorder was one of 13 exploratory covariates (Methods › Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: psychiatric medicines were tapered before baseline; the primary outcome was assessed 6 to 8 weeks after the third session.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo with identical therapy (Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized 1:1, stratified by site, by an interactive web randomization system on a centralized schedule from an independent third-party vendor (Methods › Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph). Baseline characteristics were broadly similar, but more placebo participants were female at birth (82.4% vs 60.4%; editors' P = .013 by chi-square, .017 by Fisher's test); female sex was associated with better outcomes irrespective of treatment (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 2nd paragraph), so this imbalance would favour the placebo arm. Comorbid major depression 100% vs 92.5%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; treatment expectancy was not measured (Discussion, 8th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: CAPS-5 total severity; key secondary: SDS; both by blinded independent assessors by video at baseline, after sessions 1 and 2 and 6 to 8 weeks after session 3 (18 weeks after baseline). Exploratory: response (a fall of 10 points or more, agreed with the FDA as clinically meaningful), loss of diagnosis (a fall of 10 points or more and no longer meeting the diagnostic criteria), remission (CAPS-5 of 11 or less and no longer meeting the criteria) and 13 covariates. Blinding survey at study termination (visit 20). Safety: treatment-emergent adverse events (first experimental session to last integration session) with severity graded by the site physician, serious events, events of special interest (cardiac events that could indicate QT prolongation or arrhythmia; suicide risk; terms for misuse, diversion, dependence or overdose), C-SSRS at each visit, vital signs (Methods › Randomization and masking, 3rd paragraph; Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Adverse events of special interest).
outcomes.validity_norms: Assessors were trained and supervised by independent consultants with PTSD-diagnostic expertise, who reviewed each assessor's first two assessments and 20% of all assessments; inter-rater reliability statistics are not given in the main text (Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a larger fall in CAPS-5 from baseline to 18 weeks on MDMA, estimated by MMRM with treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction and dissociative subtype as fixed effects and baseline CAPS-5 as a covariate, using the de jure estimand of the modified ITT population (at least one exposure and one follow-up CAPS-5), with the de facto (treatment-policy) estimand as support; missing observations assumed missing at random and the assumption tested with a tipping-point analysis described only in the Supplementary Methods (not read) (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Alpha 0.0499 for the two-sided primary and secondary tests after an administrative interim analysis for sample-size re-estimation; the main text does not describe a testing hierarchy; the three responder categories and the 13 exploratory covariates (alpha 0.0499 each) were not adjusted. The count of 5 covers CAPS-5, SDS and the three responder categories (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Assessors were blinded to the general design, visit, assignment, number of treatments and safety data, vetted for conflicts of interest, told not to read or attend presentations on MDMA-assisted therapy, and did no more than one CAPS-5 per participant; participants were asked not to share their opinion of their assignment (Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd paragraph). Whether assessors could guess allocation is not reported. In the end-of-study survey, 49 of 52 on MDMA (94.2%) were certain or thought they had received MDMA, 1 (1.9%) thought placebo and 2 (3.8%) could not tell; 33 of 44 on placebo (75.0%) were certain or thought they had received placebo, 9 (20.5%) thought MDMA and 2 (4.5%) could not tell; most on MDMA gave positive mental or emotional effects (45 of 52) and positive physical effects (29 of 52) as their reasons, most on placebo no effect (28 of 44) (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph). The survey's respondents were 52 of 53 on MDMA and 44 of 51 on placebo; whether the eight who did not answer are the eight who stopped treatment is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: De jure MMRM: least-squares mean change in CAPS-5 −23.7 (95% CI −26.94 to −20.44) on MDMA vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28) on placebo; treatment difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), P < 0.001; d = 0.7; within-group d 1.95 and 1.25; de facto −23.7 (−26.97 to −20.47) vs −14.8 (−18.24 to −11.33), P < 0.001 (Results › Primary outcomes). SDS: −3.3 (−4.03 to −2.60) vs −2.1 (−2.89 to −1.33); difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14), P = 0.03, d = 0.4 (Results › Secondary outcomes). At 18 weeks, among those assessed: response 45 of 52 (86.5%) vs 29 of 42 (69.0%); loss of diagnosis 37 of 52 (71.2%) vs 20 of 42 (47.6%); remission 24 of 52 (46.2%) vs 9 of 42 (21.4%); numbers needed to treat as printed: six for response, four for loss of diagnosis and four for remission (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 1st paragraph). Editors' calculations with everyone randomized as the denominator (those without an 18-week assessment counted as not improved): response 84.9% vs 56.9% (difference 28.0 points, 95% CI 11.4 to 44.7); loss of diagnosis 69.8% vs 39.2% (30.6, 12.4 to 48.8); remission 45.3% vs 17.6% (27.6, 10.6 to 44.6). Editors' Bang blinding index from the survey (correct minus incorrect guesses over all respondents; 0 = chance, 1 = all correct): 0.92 on MDMA and 0.55 on placebo.
analysis.covariates: Baseline CAPS-5 and dissociative subtype in the primary model. Of 13 exploratory covariates, only lifetime SSRI use interacted with treatment (better MDMA effect, P = 0.02); female sex and a baseline BDI-II of 23 or more were associated with better outcomes in both arms (P < 0.05); details only in Supplementary Table 5 (not read) (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: NCT04077437, submitted 30 August 2019 and posted 4 September 2019, a year before the start (2 September 2020); the registered primary outcome (change in CAPS-5 to 18 weeks) and secondary outcome (adapted SDS) match the article (registry record). The 10-point threshold for clinically meaningful change was agreed with the FDA through a Special Protocol Assessment (Methods › Outcomes, 2nd paragraph); the protocol and statistical analysis plan are said to be available via Nature Medicine (Contributions; not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: Supplementary Tables 1 to 9 and Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2 (PDF: discontinuations, SDS domains, covariates, the blinding survey table, cardiac and blood-pressure data, suicidality events) and the source data spreadsheets were not read; analyses by gender were not planned. No outcome after 18 weeks is reported.
analysis.power: 90% power at alpha 0.0499 (assumptions not given in the main text); an administrative interim analysis for sample-size re-estimation after full enrollment and 60% of primary end-point data (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With identical therapy in both arms, CAPS-5 fell by 23.7 points on MDMA and 14.8 on placebo, a difference of 8.9 points (95% CI 4.1 to 13.7) at 18 weeks; functional impairment improved by 1.2 points more on MDMA (0 to 10 scale; 0.1 to 2.3). Among those assessed, 71% vs 48% no longer met PTSD criteria (70% vs 39% of everyone randomized, editors' calculation). At the end of the study 94% of the MDMA arm and 75% of the placebo arm identified their allocation, and expectancy was not measured. One person stopped treatment on MDMA and eight on placebo. Muscle tightness, nausea, decreased appetite and hyperhidrosis were more frequent on MDMA; there were no serious adverse events; severe events occurred in 5 vs 2 participants.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that MDMA-AT reduced PTSD symptoms and functional impairment in a diverse population and was generally well tolerated (Abstract). The Discussion argues that “several observations support expectancy mitigation in the current study” (Discussion, 8th paragraph): the groups did not separate after the first session, placebo dropouts did not all occur after the first session, and not all participants identified their treatment; but 5 of the 8 placebo dropouts did stop after the first session (Fig. 1), Fig. 3 already shows 39.6% vs 22.0% with loss of diagnosis after the first session (although the CAPS-5 means in Fig. 2a are only about 3 points apart at that visit, with standard-error bars that nearly meet, which fits the authors' reading for the continuous score; editors' reading of the image), and 94% and 75% identified their allocation. The low dropout on MDMA is read as a true shift in participant engagement, although the authors also name disappointment from ineffective blinding as a possible reason for the placebo dropouts (Discussion, 3rd paragraph). The authors acknowledge that superiority over SSRIs cannot be assumed, that the evaluation did not extend beyond 2 months after therapy, and that the large improvement on placebo with therapy may reflect the therapy itself (Discussion, 5th to 7th paragraphs). Statements on phase 2 safety, dropout and durability cite the pooled phase 2 analyses (references 13 and 32) that were retracted in 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025).

timeline.event: Mithoefer et al., pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (reference 13), cited for phase 2 risk and benefit and dropout; retracted in August 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025); not read here.

Jerome et al., pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials (reference 32), cited for continuing improvement after 12 months and for common adverse events; retracted in August 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025); not read here.
MAPP1, the first phase 3 trial, same sponsor and design: CAPS-5 difference 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) in 90 adults with severe PTSD; blinding not assessed.
This trial (MAPP2), published 14 September 2023: CAPS-5 difference 8.9 points (4.1 to 13.7) in 104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD.
Author Correction (7 October 2024): 14 members of the MAPP2 Study Collaborator Group added to the main list of collaborators; no other change described.
Brett & Bynum, systematic review without meta-analysis of six MAPS-related randomized trials, including this one.

replication.where_it_stands: MAPP2 reproduces the direction and significance of MAPP1's primary and secondary results with a smaller standardized effect (d 0.7 vs 0.91) in a broader, more diverse sample; both trials come from the same sponsor, design, therapy manual and many of the same investigators, so they are not independent replications. No active-comparator or independent trial exists in the sources read, and no outcome beyond 18 weeks is reported; the authors name an ongoing long-term follow-up study (NCT05066282).

what_would_settle_it: An independent, preregistered trial with an active comparator that produces noticeable effects (or several MDMA doses), expectancy measured before treatment, blinding checked during treatment rather than only at the end, assessors' guesses recorded, adverse events collected by staff independent of the therapy team, and follow-up for at least 12 months; and a comparison with a trauma-focused psychotherapy of matched therapist time.

domains.note: Central interactive web randomization on a schedule from an independent vendor, stratified by site; allocation concealed. More women in the placebo arm (82% vs 60%, P = .013 to .017, editors' calculation), compatible with chance; because female sex predicted better outcomes in both arms, this imbalance would if anything favour placebo.

Most participants knew their allocation by the end (94% and 75% correct identification), and therapists probably did too. Six placebo participants chose to stop treatment against none on MDMA before the third session, consistent with awareness; the de jure estimand drops 11 off-treatment placebo measurements, but the de facto analysis that includes them gave the same estimates.

The primary end point is available for 52 of 53 on MDMA (98%) and 42 of 51 on placebo (82%) in the de jure analysis; placebo discontinuation was probably related to perceived lack of benefit, so data may not be missing at random; a tipping-point analysis is described only in the unread Supplementary Methods. If placebo participants who stopped were doing worse, leaving them out would favour placebo, biasing toward no difference.

The assessors were blinded and independent, but the CAPS-5 rests on participants' reports and most participants knew their allocation (94% on MDMA, 75% on placebo at study end, most citing the effects they felt or did not feel); expectancy was not measured and assessors' guesses were not reported. Knowledge of allocation could plausibly have influenced reported symptoms; its size cannot be estimated from the data.
Prospectively registered; the registered primary and secondary outcomes and the stated analysis are those reported; de jure and de facto estimates agree.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A prospectively registered, carefully conducted confirmatory trial with blinded independent assessors and low attrition on MDMA. The overall judgment is high because of the outcome-measurement domain: most participants identified their allocation and the primary outcome rests on their reports, while expectancy was not measured. Differential dropout (1 vs 8) adds some concern but probably biases toward the null. The trial can be cited for a larger fall in clinician-rated PTSD symptoms and a smaller gain in function with MDMA than with placebo plus the same therapy over 18 weeks, for the blinding survey, and for common adverse events; it cannot be cited for an effect of MDMA separate from expectancy, for durability, for comparison with other treatments, or for rare or delayed harms.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 324 screened, 121 enrolled, 104 randomized (53 MDMA, 51 placebo); stopped treatment 1 on MDMA (1.9%) and 8 on placebo (15.7%: 6 chose to stop, 2 because of adverse events); 52 and 42 in the de jure analysis at 18 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline, MDMA vs placebo: female at birth 32 (60.4%) vs 42 (82.4%); Hispanic or Latino 17 (32.1%) vs 11 (21.6%); White 37 (69.8%) vs 32 (62.7%); baseline CAPS-5 39.4 (6.6) vs 38.7 (6.7); moderate PTSD 13 (24.5%) vs 15 (29.4%); dissociative subtype 13 (24.5%) vs 11 (21.6%); comorbid major depression 49 (92.5%) vs 51 (100%); lifetime MDMA use 22 (41.5%) vs 26 (51.0%). Overall 35 of 104 (33.7%) other than White, 28 of 104 (26.9%) Hispanic or Latino; mean PTSD duration 16.2 (13.3) years.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary end point, de jure MMRM: least-squares mean change in CAPS-5 from baseline to 18 weeks −23.7 (95% CI −26.94 to −20.44) on MDMA vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28) on placebo; treatment difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), P < 0.001; d = 0.7 (within-group d 1.95 and 1.25); de facto estimand −23.7 (−26.97 to −20.47) vs −14.8 (−18.24 to −11.33), P < 0.001.
Key secondary end point, SDS: least-squares mean change −3.3 (95% CI −4.03 to −2.60) vs −2.1 (−2.89 to −1.33); treatment difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14), P = 0.03, d = 0.4.

At 18 weeks, among those assessed: response (a fall of 10 points or more) 45 of 52 (86.5%) on MDMA vs 29 of 42 (69.0%) on placebo; loss of diagnosis 37 of 52 (71.2%) vs 20 of 42 (47.6%); remission 24 of 52 (46.2%) vs 9 of 42 (21.4%); printed numbers needed to treat six, four and four. Fig. 3 prints, after the first session, loss of diagnosis in 39.6% on MDMA vs 22.0% on placebo and response in 52.8% vs 42.0%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exploratory outcomes, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 (values printed on the bars)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with everyone randomized as the denominator: response 84.9% vs 56.9%, loss of diagnosis 69.8% vs 39.2%, remission 45.3% vs 17.6%. MAPP2 defines loss of diagnosis as a fall of 10 points or more together with no longer meeting the diagnostic criteria (Methods › Outcomes, 2nd paragraph), whereas MAPP1 uses the CAPS-5 diagnostic measure alone, so the two trials' loss-of-diagnosis figures are not defined identically.

key_findings.finding: Covariates: similar responses regardless of severity, risk of hazardous alcohol or substance use, severe adverse childhood experiences or dissociative subtype; lifetime SSRI use was the only covariate interacting with treatment (P = 0.02); female sex and baseline BDI-II of 23 or more were associated with better outcomes irrespective of treatment (P < 0.05).

Blinding survey at study termination: on placebo, 33 of 44 (75.0%) were certain or thought they had received placebo, 9 (20.5%) thought MDMA, 2 (4.5%) could not tell; on MDMA, 49 of 52 (94.2%) were certain or thought they had received MDMA, 1 (1.9%) thought placebo, 2 (3.8%) could not tell. Reasons given: positive mental or emotional effect 45 of 52 and positive physical effect 29 of 52 on MDMA; no effect 28 of 44 on placebo.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Randomization and masking, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' Bang blinding index: (49 − 1)/52 = 0.92 on MDMA and (33 − 9)/44 = 0.55 on placebo. The survey was taken at the end of the study, after participants had experienced their outcomes.

key_findings.finding: Treatment-emergent adverse events: at least one in 102 of 104 (53 of 53 on MDMA, 49 of 51 on placebo); severe 5 (9.4%) vs 2 (3.9%); serious 0 vs 0; leading to discontinuation 0 vs 2 (3.9%); at least one event of special interest 6 (11.3%) vs 3 (5.9%); no events of special interest for misuse, physical dependence or diversion.

Most common adverse events (more than 10% and at least twice as frequent on MDMA; all 17 rows of Table 2): muscle tightness 31 (58.5%) vs 13 (25.5%); nausea 24 (45.3%) vs 11 (21.6%); decreased appetite 19 (35.8%) vs 5 (9.8%); hyperhidrosis 18 (34.0%) vs 3 (5.9%); feeling hot 14 (26.4%) vs 6 (11.8%); feeling cold 11 (20.8%) vs 3 (5.9%); paresthesia 10 (18.9%) vs 1 (2.0%); chest discomfort 9 (17.0%) vs 2 (3.9%); dry mouth 9 (17.0%) vs 4 (7.8%); chills 8 (15.1%) vs 1 (2.0%); feeling jittery 8 (15.1%) vs 0; restlessness 8 (15.1%) vs 2 (3.9%); blurred vision 8 (15.1%) vs 0; bruxism 7 (13.2%) vs 1 (2.0%); nystagmus 7 (13.2%) vs 1 (2.0%); mydriasis 6 (11.3%) vs 0; tremor 6 (11.3%) vs 0.

Cardiovascular: cardiac adverse events in 7 on MDMA vs 1 on placebo, all mild (palpitations 5 (9.4%) vs 1 (2.0%); tachycardia 2 (3.8%) vs 0); vascular events in 7 vs 2, all mild except one moderate hypertension in an MDMA participant with untreated hypertension; temporary dose-dependent rises in blood pressure and pulse during sessions on MDMA, not needing intervention.

Psychiatric adverse events in 44 (83.0%) on MDMA vs 37 (72.5%) on placebo, mostly suicidal ideation, insomnia and anxiety; severe: 3 on MDMA (dissociation, flashback, grief reaction) vs 2 on placebo (agitation, anxiety). Suicidality events of special interest: 2 on MDMA (suicidal ideation, one with non-suicidal self-injury) vs 2 on placebo. Treatment-emergent active suicidal ideation with some intent (C-SSRS 4 or 5) in 3 participants (2 MDMA, 1 placebo) on 5 occasions; one MDMA participant without ideation at baseline developed it. Ideation at the final preparation session: 13 of 53 (24.5%) vs 12 of 51 (23.5%); the number with ideation never exceeded baseline in either arm.

How adverse events were recorded: treatment-emergent events were those from the first experimental session to the last integration session; severity was graded by the site physician; except for serious events, relatedness to the study drug was not assessed by investigators, to preserve blinding; events were attributed to MDMA when more than 10% and at least twice as frequent as on placebo.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Expectancy: the authors state that treatment expectancy was not measured, that it was probably high in both arms, and offer three observations as supporting expectancy mitigation (no separation after the first session; placebo dropouts not all after the first session; not all participants identified their treatment).

Exclusions and misuse: participants with any substance use disorder other than cannabis or alcohol in the 12 months before enrollment, or severe or moderate (early remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorder, were excluded; the authors state that long-term data are needed to assess the risk of misuse after study participation.
Duration: the authors state that the evaluations did not extend beyond 2 months after therapy and point to the ongoing follow-up of phase 2 and 3 participants (NCT05066282).

Registry: submitted 30 August 2019, posted 4 September 2019, start 2 September 2020; registered primary outcome change in CAPS-5 to 18 weeks, secondary adapted SDS; enrollment 121; participant flow started 53 vs 51, completed 52 vs 42; least-squares means as in the article (−23.69 vs −14.78; SDS −3.31 vs −2.11; denominators 53 and 50).

key_findings.finding: Registry adverse events (5% threshold; first experimental session to the last integrative session, about 12 weeks; 53 vs 51): no serious events; headache 38 vs 31, suicidal ideation 18 vs 21, insomnia 19 vs 15, anxiety 15 vs 12, dizziness 15 vs 8, dissociation 3 vs 0, panic attack 3 vs 1, heart rate increased 3 vs 0, binge eating 0 vs 3; no term for euphoria appears.

Author Correction (Nat Med 30, 3382, published 7 October 2024): some members of the MAPP2 Study Collaborator Group had been listed only in the Supplementary Information; Charlotte Harrison, Berra Yazar-Klosinski, Wael Garas, Darrick May, Cole Marta, Susan Walker, Elizabeth Nielson, Gregory Wells, Randall Brown, Revital Amiaz, Yair Wallach, Ray Worthy, Alia Lilienstein and Amy Emerson were added to the main list of collaborators in the HTML and PDF versions.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say 94 participants completed the study and 9 discontinued (1 MDMA, 8 placebo), which sums to 103 of 104; the CONSORT diagram shows 52 and 43 completing (95), and the registry gives completed 52 vs 42 and not completed 1 vs 9.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 3 is titled with n = 53 (MDMA) and n = 50 (placebo), but the after-session-3 percentages printed on its bars match the completer denominators used in the text (86.5% = 45 of 52; 69.0% = 29 of 42).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Fig. 3; Results › Exploratory outcomes, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The responder percentages leave out the placebo participants who stopped; with everyone randomized as the denominator the differences are larger (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says ethnically or racially diverse participants were approximately half of the sample; Table 1 gives 35 of 104 (33.7%) other than White and 28 of 104 (26.9%) Hispanic or Latino without their overlap, so the share cannot be checked from the article.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the two Table 1 figures separately; Brett & Bynum's 61% adds the two overlapping percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 ethnicity rows for the placebo arm sum to 50 of 51 (11 + 39) with no missing category.
The printed numbers needed to treat for loss of diagnosis and remission are four; from the completer counts they are 4.2 and 4.0 (editors' calculation), which would conventionally be rounded up to 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial; give the risk differences instead.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives suicidal ideation (under psychiatric disorder) in 44 of 53 on MDMA (83.0%) and 47 of 51 on placebo (92.2%), 91 of 104 in all, while Results › Safety, 5th paragraph gives 87 of 104 with a lifetime history of suicidal ideation; the article does not reconcile the two.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the figure with its place. Brett & Bynum's 87 of 104 follows the Results.

disagreements.first_pass: Assessors were blinded to the general design, visit, assignment, number of treatments and safety data, vetted for conflicts of interest, told not to read or attend presentations on MDMA-assisted therapy, and did no more than one CAPS-5 per participant; participants were asked not to share their opinion of their assignment (Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd paragraph). In the end-of-study survey, 49 of 52 on MDMA (94.2%) were certain or thought they had received MDMA, 1 (1.9%) thought placebo and 2 (3.8%) could not tell; 33 of 44 on placebo (75.0%) were certain or thought they had received placebo, 9 (20.5%) thought MDMA and 2 (4.5%) could not tell; most on MDMA gave positive mental or emotional effects (45 of 52) and positive physical effects (29 of 52) as their reasons, most on placebo no effect (28 of 44) (Results › Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph).
